analysis.one_liner: Stops carmakers from collecting, selling, or sharing your vehicle's data without your consent.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with one Republican and one Democratic sponsor in December 2024, never received a committee hearing or a vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Modern cars generate a constant stream of data: where you drive, how fast, where you park, and what you do inside the cabin. This bill would require automakers to get your clear, written, revocable consent before accessing that data, and would bar them from selling it except under a warrant, court order, emergency, or your explicit permission. It would also ban sharing Americans' personal information with governments in China, Russia, Iran, North Korea, and Venezuela. And it would require carmakers to give owners free access to their own vehicle's data through an open, technology-neutral interface, so owners could delete data, set their own preferences, and repair or program their vehicles without paying for manufacturer-only tools.
analysis.who_benefits: Vehicle owners, including drivers of farm and construction equipment, gain control over data their cars generate. Independent repair shops and aftermarket businesses gain because the bill requires a technology-neutral data interface and forbids forcing owners to buy manufacturer devices or licenses to read their vehicle's data.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Car owners and independent repair shops

how_it_helps.text: Automakers could not access operator data — everything from sensors, GPS, and onboard computers — unless the owner gives informed, written, easily withdrawn consent, or the data is used solely to improve vehicle performance or safety [S2].
Selling or sharing that data would be limited to court-ordered warrants, court orders with 48 hours' notice for the owner to object, emergency response, or the owner's express permission [S2].
Manufacturers would be banned from selling Americans' personally identifiable information — including location and internet activity — to China, Russia, Iran, North Korea, and Venezuela [S2].

Owners would get free access to and control of their vehicle's data, including open interfaces for deleting personal data and setting preferences, without paying fees, decryption licenses, or buying manufacturer-only devices [S2].

The FTC would enforce the rules as an unfair or deceptive practice, and the Commission would have to produce reports documenting who currently accesses vehicle data, who it is sold to, and how often it is compromised [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Automakers lose revenue from selling or monetizing telematics data — including to insurers and data brokers — and lose control of the repair and customization market, since owners could access their vehicles' data with any tool rather than manufacturer-approved equipment.

drawbacks.text: The bill preempts any state or federal law covering the same ground, which could override stronger state privacy protections already on the books [S2].

The exception allowing manufacturers to access data 'solely to improve covered vehicle performance or safety' without consent is broad, and automakers could argue much of what they collect qualifies [S2].

Compliance costs — building open, secure, standards-based data interfaces under FTC-set standards — would fall on manufacturers and could be passed into vehicle prices, while the FTC must fund oversight from existing funds with no new appropriations [S2].
Enforcement runs only through the FTC; the bill creates no private right of action, so individual owners could not sue on their own [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary drivers the trade is strongly favorable: the bill trades a modest compliance cost borne by a concentrated industry for a substantial privacy right and open access to data owners already paid for. Its real weaknesses are the broad performance-and-safety exception, which a motivated manufacturer could drive a truck through, and federal preemption that could erase stronger state protections.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate in December 2024, sent to the Commerce Committee, and never taken up before the Congress ended three weeks later.

narrative.text: Sen. Mike Lee (R-UT) introduced the bill on December 18, 2024, joined by Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-OR) as its sole cosponsor [S1][S3].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, which was its last action [S4].
The committee held no hearing, marked up nothing, and the full Senate never voted; the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, killing the bill [S1][S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers and the businesses that buy vehicle data from them are better off, because nothing now limits how they collect, use, or sell information from cars on the road today.

for.name: Sen. Mike Lee
for.role: U.S. Senator from Utah; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced S. 5579 on December 18, 2024, barring manufacturers from accessing or selling vehicle data without owner consent and requiring open owner access to vehicle data.

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-WA)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — so it never reached the Senate floor before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had one Republican sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor, but with no committee action or vote there is no record of how the parties would have lined up.

industries.note: Carmakers would lose the ability to collect and sell telematics data — location, driving behavior, cabin activity — without consent, and would have to build open data interfaces that undercut manufacturer-controlled repair and customization. Their gain from the status quo comes at the expense of owners' privacy and repair freedom.
Businesses that buy driving and location data from carmakers would lose their supply, since sales would require explicit owner permission or legal process.

industries.industry: Independent repair shops and aftermarket equipment makers
industries.note: The technology-neutral, no-fee access requirement would let independent shops read vehicle data without manufacturer licenses or proprietary devices.
